title: Restoring Meaning: AI and Education for a Life of Inquiry Education Wegerif, Rupert
author: Wegerif, Rupert
summary: Rupert Wegerif uses the arrival of generative AI as an occasion to revisit the most fundamental question about education: what is it actually for? His answer is that education's purpose has always been the formation of persons into meaning-making communities -- and that this formation happens not through conscious reasoning alone but through embodiment, relationship, language, and shared ritual that shape the self long before it can articulate its own beliefs. Modern secular education, Wegerif argues, has drifted into a culture of total work (mediated assessment, credentialism, competition) that leaves students with only one coherent path to meaning -- individual success -- producing anxiety and isolation rather than belonging and purpose. He draws a counterintuitive lesson from religious traditions: their superior wellbeing outcomes are not an argument for confessionalism but a signal that formation through shared practice, ritual, and community is something secular institutions must learn to replicate. The article's strongest claim is that social media and AI are already forming human beings whether we choose to think about it or not, and the relevant question is whether we can consciously and collectively take responsibility for the culture that forms us. AI, used deliberately, could support expanded collective inquiry, dialogues across cultural traditions, and forms of shared practice that reconnect learners to purposes larger than individual achievement.
points: * Formation -- the shaping of persons through embodied practice, language, ritual, and relationship -- always happens, consciously or not; what education must do is take deliberate responsibility for the culture that shapes students rather than pretending to be a neutral instrument of information transfer. * Modern secular education's hidden curriculum transmits a single message: meaning comes from individual success measured through assessment and credential -- producing the very anxiety, isolation, and purpose-deficit it claims to be solving. * Religious communities' superior wellbeing outcomes (lower depression, addiction, suicide, stronger belonging) are not evidence for theology but evidence that formation through shared practice, ritual, and community produces psychological goods that purely cognitive education cannot replicate. * The self is not prior to formation and capable of rationally consenting to its own shaping -- it emerges through formation; the worry about social media and AI should not be about autonomy violation but about whether the formation those platforms deliver is one we have chosen collectively. * AI's educational potential is not primarily more-efficient content delivery but support for expanded collective inquiry -- connecting learners across cultures around shared human questions, staging dialogues between traditions, enabling practices of reflection that reconnect individuals to humanity's ongoing conversation about truth and meaning. quotes: Human beings are shaped pre-reflectively through embodiment, relationships, language, ritual, and culture long before they are able to articulate beliefs about themselves or the world. It is through induction into forms of life, within families, communities, friendships, and institutions, that we first learn who we are, what matters, whether the world is trustworthy, and whether life is worth living.

Into this vacuum students are offered only one clear path to meaning: personal success. Whether in school exam results or comparisons of lifestyles on TikTok, it becomes clear that being ordinary is not enough. The results are visible. Not wisdom or belonging, but anxiety, isolation, and the sense that meaning must be manufactured alone against a universe that offers none of its own.

We humans are always already formed through language, education, institutions, media, and relationships. This is not a failure of freedom. It is the condition through which meaning and freedom become possible. The self is not prior to formation but emerges through it.
The question, then, is not whether technology shapes us. It always will. The question is whether we can consciously and collectively take responsibility for shaping the culture that shapes us.

Used well, AI could help education recover what modern institutions have partly lost. It could connect learners across cultures around shared human questions, stage dialogues between traditions separated by language and history, and enable forms of collective inquiry at scales previously impossible.

AI tutors, moderators, and social platforms could instead be designed to reward curiosity, listening, intellectual humility, courage in questioning assumptions, collaborative problem-solving, and sustained inquiry.

The educational challenge of the age of AI is therefore not simply how to use new tools efficiently. It is whether education can help cultivate forms of collective intelligence and collective wisdom capable not only of sustaining but also of calling into being a self-reflective, self-organising, and consciously self-evolving planetary culture."
